options.a: Maintain steering control during hard braking on slippery surfaces
options.b: Shorten stopping distances on loose gravel and fresh snow-covered roads
options.c: Prevent every skid even when the driver enters a curve too fast
options.d: Replace the need to maintain safe following distance

distractorExplanations.b: On loose gravel or fresh snow ABS can lengthen stops because locked wheels would build a wedge of material; its real benefit is steering control.
distractorExplanations.c: “Prevent every skid even when the driver enters a curve too fast” is incorrect because aBS prevents wheel lockup so the driver can steer while braking hard; it does not guarantee shorter stops on every surface.
distractorExplanations.d: “Replace the need to maintain safe following distance” is incorrect because aBS prevents wheel lockup so the driver can steer while braking hard; it does not guarantee shorter stops on every surface.

options.a: Shut off the engine immediately while still in the traffic lane
options.b: Increase speed to force more air through the radiator
options.c: Open the hot radiator cap to check coolant
options.d: Pull off safely, idle to cool if safe, and investigate

distractorExplanations.a: Shutting down in a live travel lane creates a collision hazard; get clear of traffic first, then idle or shut down as conditions allow.
distractorExplanations.b: Higher speed increases load and may worsen overheating.
distractorExplanations.c: Opening a hot, pressurized radiator can spray scalding coolant; let the system cool before checking the level.

options.a: One second for each 10 feet of vehicle length under 40 mph
options.b: One second for each 15 feet of vehicle length at speeds under 40 mph
options.c: One second for each 20 feet of vehicle length at any speed
options.d: A fixed four-second gap, the same as a passenger car

distractorExplanations.b: The manual rule is one second per 10 feet under 40 mph; one second per 15 feet leaves a third less time than required.
distractorExplanations.c: One second per 20 feet halves the manual's minimum and ignores the extra second needed above 40 mph.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavy vehicles need length-based time—one second per 10 feet plus one more above 40 mph—not a fixed car-style gap.

options.a: Drafting beside a car reduces your truck's wind resistance and fuel use
options.b: They may change lanes into you without seeing your vehicle
options.c: It blocks your view of the road shoulder on that side
options.d: It forces you to brake harder when traffic ahead slows

distractorExplanations.a: Riding alongside another vehicle gives no meaningful drag or fuel benefit; the real risk is that its driver cannot see you and merges into you.
distractorExplanations.c: The concern is the other driver's view, not yours; lingering where they cannot see you invites a lane change into your rig.
distractorExplanations.d: Braking depends on space ahead; the blind-spot problem is that the other driver may merge into you without warning.

options.a: To prevent cargo from shifting or falling
options.b: To keep axle weights within legal limits
options.c: To protect the cargo itself from shipping damage
options.d: To set the shipper's liability for loads

distractorExplanations.c: Damage protection is a commercial concern for the shipper; FMCSA securement rules exist to stop shifting and falling loads that cause crashes.
distractorExplanations.b: Axle limits come from weight laws and load placement; securement rules control movement of the load.
distractorExplanations.d: Liability is covered by the bill of lading and contracts; securement rules target road safety from shifting or falling cargo.

options.a: To prevent cargo from moving forward, backward, or sideways
options.b: To distribute weight evenly over the axles to stay within legal limits
options.c: To protect cargo surfaces from tiedown strap damage
options.d: To lower the cargo's center of gravity on the trailer deck

distractorExplanations.b: Axle weight distribution is handled by where cargo is placed; blocking and bracing restrain cargo against movement in transit.
distractorExplanations.c: Edge protectors guard cargo from straps; blocking and bracing are restraints that keep cargo from moving.
distractorExplanations.d: Blocking and bracing do not change load height; they fill gaps and restrain cargo so it cannot shift.

options.a: Increase traction by putting more weight on the drive axles
options.b: Lower the center of gravity and improve stability
options.c: Reduce the number of tiedowns the cargo requires
options.d: Shorten stopping distance on wet roads

distractorExplanations.a: Drive-axle loading depends on fore-aft position, not height; keeping cargo low and centered mainly lowers the center of gravity.
distractorExplanations.c: Tiedown count is set by cargo length and weight rules; low, centered placement improves stability, not securement count.
distractorExplanations.d: Stopping distance is driven by speed, weight and brakes; load height mainly affects rollover and handling.
